etymology: Hebrew ra‘meses, of Egyptian origin, perhaps “son of Ra” or “begotten of the sun,” a store-city of Egypt and the place whence Israel began their journey out of bondage.
biblical_def: Rameses was a store-city of the land of Egypt, one of the treasure cities which the children of Israel built for Pharaoh in their bondage, and it became the starting-point of the great march out of the house of slavery (Exo 1:11; Exo 12:37). On the morrow after the passover, on the fifteenth day of the first month, Israel departed from Rameses with an high hand, journeying to Succoth, about six hundred thousand on foot that were men, beside children (Num 33:3). It is a marvel of the providence of God that the very city the Hebrews had built with rigour for their oppressor became the threshold of their liberty, for the LORD turned the place of their toil into the gate of their deliverance. The dictionary marks Rameses not as a contested matter of doctrine, but as a real city set down by the Spirit of God to fix the beginning of the redemption He wrought with a stretched-out arm. He who appointed the bounds of their habitation appointed also the day and the place of their going forth. Rameses stands as a witness that the LORD brings His people out of the very midst of their affliction, and that the redemption of Israel from Egypt is a figure of the greater exodus wherein Christ leads His own out of the bondage of sin into the liberty of the sons of God.

etymology: Hebrew sukkoth, “booths” or “tents,” the first encampment of Israel after their departure from Rameses in the going out of Egypt.
biblical_def: Succoth was the first station of Israel’s wilderness march, the place whither they journeyed from Rameses on the day they went out of Egypt, and they removed from Succoth and pitched in Etham, in the edge of the wilderness (Num 33:5-6; Exo 13:20). The name signifies “booths” or “tents,” and it is the same word by which Jacob long before named a place where he built him an house and made booths for his cattle. Here, at the very first remove out of bondage, Israel learned that they were now a pilgrim people, dwelling in tents and following the cloud whither the LORD should lead them. The dictionary marks Succoth not as a matter of dispute, but as a real camp set down by the Spirit of God in the careful record of the journeys of the children of Israel. He who brought them out appointed every stage of their going, the first booth as surely as the last. There is grace here, for the saints of God are still a tabernacling people, who confess that they are strangers and pilgrims on the earth and seek a city which hath foundations. Succoth stands as a witness that the LORD orders the pilgrimage of His people from the first night of their freedom, and that the booth in the wilderness is dearer to the redeemed than the brick-kilns of Egypt.

etymology: Hebrew ’etham, perhaps of Egyptian origin signifying “fort” or “wall of the sea,” a station of Israel in the edge of the wilderness.
biblical_def: Etham was the second station of the wilderness march, the camp in the edge of the wilderness whither Israel journeyed from Succoth, and it was here that the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud and by night in a pillar of fire (Num 33:6-8; Exo 13:20-21). From Etham they turned again, as the LORD commanded, unto Pi-hahiroth before the sea, and afterward, in the after journeys, they passed through the midst of the sea into the wilderness, and went three days’ journey in the wilderness of Etham, and pitched in Marah. The name marks the border-land between the settled country and the trackless waste, the place where Israel stood upon the edge of the great unknown with no guide but the LORD Himself. The dictionary marks Etham not as a disputed matter, but as a real camp set down by the Spirit of God in the record of the journeys. He who led them appointed even the edge of the wilderness for their resting, and there gave them the pillar of cloud and of fire, that they should never be without His presence. Etham stands as a witness that the LORD goes before His people into the wilderness, and that the edge of the unknown is no terror to those whom the Shepherd of Israel leads, for the cloud of His presence is over them in the day and the fire of His presence about them in the night.

etymology: Hebrew pi ha-chiroth, perhaps “mouth of the gorges” or “place where sedge grows,” the station of Israel before the Red Sea, between Migdol and the sea.
biblical_def: Pi-hahiroth was the station before the Red Sea, between Migdol and the sea, over against Baal-zephon, where the LORD commanded Israel to turn and encamp, that He might be honoured upon Pharaoh and all his host (Num 33:7-8; Exo 14:2,9). It was a place of seeming peril, the sea before them and the mountains about them and the chariots of Egypt behind, where the people cried out in their fear and said it had been better to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness. Yet the LORD had appointed the very strait on purpose, that the children of Israel should stand still and see the salvation of the LORD, who divided the sea and made them go over on dry ground, and overthrew Pharaoh in the deep. The dictionary marks Pi-hahiroth not as a contested matter, but as a real camp set down by the Spirit of God where the great deliverance at the sea was wrought. He who led them into the strait led them through it, that His arm might be known. Pi-hahiroth stands as a witness that the LORD often brings His people into places of extremity, hemmed in and helpless to all sight, that He may show forth His salvation; for the same God who shut Israel up between Migdol and the sea opened them a way through the waters, and that passage is a figure of the redemption Christ works for His own.

etymology: Hebrew dophqah, perhaps “a knocking” or “cattle-driving,” a station of Israel in the wilderness between the Red Sea and Sinai.
biblical_def: Dophkah was a station of Israel in the wilderness, the camp whither they journeyed after they removed from the Red Sea, when they had departed from the wilderness of Sin, and from Dophkah they removed and pitched in Alush (Num 33:12-13). Of this place the Scripture records nothing beyond its name and its order in the journeys, no murmuring and no miracle, only that Israel came thither and removed thence under the leading of the cloud. The dictionary does not invent a history where the LORD was pleased to leave silence; it honours that the Spirit of God set down even the quiet, uneventful camps in the careful register of the march. For not every station of the pilgrimage was a Marah of bitter waters or a Rephidim of striving; many were but the plain and unremembered removes from one resting-place to the next. There is grace here, for the life of the people of God is made up largely of such ordinary stages, days neither of great trial nor of great wonder, yet all of them ordered and numbered by the LORD. Dophkah stands as a witness that He who led Israel kept the reckoning of every camp, the obscure as faithfully as the famous; and the saint whose days pass without remark may know that his quiet pilgrimage is written too in the book of God’s faithful keeping of His own.

biblical_def: Alush was a station of Israel in the wilderness, the camp whither they journeyed when they departed from Dophkah, and from Alush they removed and pitched in Rephidim, where was no water for the people to drink (Num 33:13-14). Of Alush itself the Scripture records nothing save its name and its place in the order of the journeys, neither murmuring nor mercy marked upon it, only that the cloud rested there and then went forward. The journeys of Israel were forty years and more, and many of the stages were silent removes from one barren resting-place to the next, days that left no record but were numbered every one by the God who led them. There is comfort here for the people of God, whose pilgrimage is likewise filled with such quiet, unremarkable stations. Alush stands as a witness that the LORD kept faithful account of every camp, the unknown as surely as the renowned, and that the saint whose path winds through many an obscure and unremembered place is led by the same Shepherd who brought Israel from Alush to Rephidim, and at last to the rest He had prepared.

etymology: Hebrew qibroth ha-ta’avah, “the graves of lust” or “the graves of craving,” the station where the people who lusted after flesh were buried in the wilderness.
biblical_def: Kibroth-hattaavah was a station of Israel in the wilderness whose very name signifies “the graves of lust,” for there they buried the people that lusted, who had loathed the manna and wept for flesh, saying, Who shall give us flesh to eat? (Num 11:34; Num 33:16). The LORD gave them quails from the sea in their craving, but while the meat was yet between their teeth, ere it was chewed, His wrath was kindled, and He smote them with a very great plague, and they called the name of the place the graves of lust because there they buried the people that had lusted. From Kibroth-hattaavah the people journeyed unto Hazeroth and abode there. The dictionary marks this place not as a contested matter, but as a real camp where the Spirit of God set down a solemn warning written into the very ground. The lusting after Egypt’s flesh was at heart a despising of the LORD who was among them, and the graves of lust stand as a monument to the peril of an unbelieving and discontented heart. Kibroth-hattaavah is a witness that the LORD will be sanctified in His people, and that the craving which sets the belly above His provision digs its own grave; whereof the apostle warns the saints that they lust not after evil things, as they also lusted, but learn in whatsoever state they are therewith to be content.

etymology: Hebrew chatseroth, “enclosures” or “settlements,” a station of Israel where Miriam was struck with leprosy for speaking against Moses.
biblical_def: Hazeroth was a station of Israel in the wilderness whither the people journeyed from Kibroth-hattaavah and abode there, and it was here that Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married (Num 11:35; Num 12:1; Num 33:17). They said, Hath the LORD indeed spoken only by Moses? hath he not spoken also by us? and the LORD heard it. He came down in the pillar of the cloud and rebuked them, declaring that with His servant Moses He spake mouth to mouth, and His anger was kindled, and when the cloud departed, behold, Miriam became leprous, white as snow. Moses cried unto the LORD, Heal her now, O God, I beseech thee, and she was shut out of the camp seven days, and the people journeyed not till Miriam was brought in again. The dictionary marks Hazeroth not as a contested matter, but as a real camp where the Spirit of God set down a grave warning against the sin of envying the LORD’s appointed servant. Hazeroth stands as a witness that the LORD defends His own anointed and resents the murmuring tongue, yet hears the cry of intercession and is full of mercy; for He struck Miriam in justice but healed her at the prayer of meek Moses, and so taught Israel to fear His honour and to seek His grace.

etymology: Hebrew rithmah, “place of the broom-shrub” or “juniper,” from rothem, the desert broom, a station of Israel in the wilderness after Hazeroth.
biblical_def: Rithmah was a station of Israel in the wilderness, the camp whither they journeyed when they departed from Hazeroth, and from Rithmah they removed and pitched at Rimmon-parez (Num 33:18-19). The name comes from the rothem, the desert broom or juniper, under whose meagre shade the weary Elijah once lay down and asked that he might die, and beneath which the wanderer of the waste found such shelter as the barren places afford. Of Rithmah itself the Scripture records nothing but its name and its order in the journeys, a place known only by the lowly shrub that grew there. The dictionary will not feign a history where the LORD gave only a name; it honours that the Spirit of God set down even this place of the broom-bush in the careful register of the march. There is a quiet mercy in such names, for the LORD appointed His people resting-places marked by the humblest of growing things, and provided shade in the desert where to the eye there was none. Rithmah stands as a witness that He who led Israel through the great and terrible wilderness knew every juniper and every broom that grew along the way, and that the God who notes the shrub of the waste notes also the path of His pilgrim people, leading them by stations both named and nameless toward their rest.

etymology: Hebrew rissah, perhaps “ruin” or “dew, dropping,” a station of Israel in the wilderness between Libnah and Kehelathah.
biblical_def: Rissah was a station of Israel in the wilderness, the camp whither they journeyed when they departed from Libnah, and from Rissah they removed and pitched in Kehelathah (Num 33:21-22). Of this place the Scripture records nothing beyond its name and its order in the long register of the journeys, neither sign nor murmuring marked upon it, only that Israel came thither and removed thence as the cloud went before them. The dictionary will not invent a history where the LORD was pleased to leave silence; it honours that the Spirit of God thought it good to set down even this hidden camp in the faithful reckoning of the march. The pilgrimage of Israel was a long succession of such removes, many of them nameless to memory and bare of any recorded event, yet every one numbered and appointed by the God who led them. There is comfort here for the people of God, whose own journey is largely made of such unremarked stages. Rissah stands as a witness that the LORD kept exact account of every camp, the obscure as faithfully as the famous, and that He who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people appointed also each resting-place of His redeemed; so that the saint whose path passes through many a forgotten station may trust the Shepherd who leads, and not one camp of the way is lost from the book of His remembrance.
